1	# Spec-Driven Product Working Procedures — a portable playbook
2	
3	This document defines **how the owner wants a spec-driven product project run**, as a **bootstrap to
4	drop into a new project of this class** from day one. The class: **build and ship a small end-user
5	product against an executable specification — every requirement is a numbered leaf claimed by exactly
6	one executable proof of the right kind, expected results are owned by the owner, and releases cut
7	automatically while `main` stays green.** The archetype is a UI-centric product (a browser-extension
8	panel, a small web or mobile app) and the examples lean that way, but the discipline applies wherever
9	observable behavior can be specified leaf by leaf — read "surface", "render", and "server" as whatever
10	they mean for your project.
11	
12	It is written to be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
13	product, stack, or harness specifics of any particular project. Those live elsewhere — platform
14	gotchas in the project's technology packs, release mechanics in its release pack or release doc, and
15	the concrete spec, harness, and commands in the project's own docs. General test-trust practices
16	(see-it-fail, snapshot hygiene, the re-baselining approval procedure, capture-artifact-first) are
17	corpus canon in the writing-tests skill; this pack assumes them and adds the class's development loop
18	on top.
19	
20	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**: when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and drop it;
21	when the project needs a rule this document lacks, add it in the project's own docs first. The
22	non-negotiable is the spirit: **the spec is executable, the expecteds belong to the owner, the real
23	code produces every actual, and the product ships on green.**
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 1. The executable spec is the backbone
28	
29	- **One numbered requirements document states what the product must do**, leaf by leaf: what each
30	  surface must render, how it must behave, the exact copy and semantics it must carry. Not prose
31	  aspirations — specific, testable statements.
32	- **Keep the spec's boundary crisp: a leaf is what the harness can assert.** The feature-level story —
33	  what the product does and why — lives in the product's prose docs; the spec holds the specific,
34	  testable statements (exact strings, placement, semantics). A statement no kind can prove isn't a
35	  leaf yet: it stays prose, or it's the trigger to add the kind that can prove it.
36	- **Every leaf carries a stable id.** Add new requirements under new numbers; never renumber or reuse
37	  a retired one — the ids are what cases, commits, and review discussion key on.
38	- **Doc-first, red by default.** Adding a leaf with no executable proof fails the build until a case
39	  claims it.
40	- **The spec drives the tests, never the other way around.** A behavior change starts by editing the
41	  leaf, watching the gate go red, then changing product and proof to match. A test changed without its
42	  leaf — or a leaf reworded to match what the code happens to do — inverts the authority.
43	
44	## 2. Every leaf ⇄ exactly one proof, of the right kind
45	
46	- **Enforce the bijection with a committed coverage gate**: each leaf claimed by exactly one case,
47	  each case claiming exactly one leaf, and every discovered kind of case actually executed by a
48	  runner. The gate is part of the project's own suite.
49	- **A *kind* is one way a requirement can be asserted** — a rendered-state snapshot, a driven gesture,
50	  a pure rule, a boundary-enforced rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually observe what it
51	  asserts. Keep kinds **extensible** — adding one is a self-contained drop.
52	- **A kind may be a singleton.** "The product loads in the real environment" is a perfectly good leaf
53	  whose mechanism is one end-to-end case; the kind names the *way of asserting*, not a population of
54	  cases.
55	- **Give each kind's runner a named lane, and keep the default lane fast and deterministic.** Heavy
56	  real-environment kinds gate the merge from CI without slowing the inner loop; their trust rules
57	  (twice-green before merging, self-diagnosing on failure) are canon in the writing-tests skill.
58	- **Actuals come from the real code.** Whatever the kind, the proof drives the shipped entry points
59	  under a faithful harness — never a parallel re-implementation of what production "should" do (the
60	  writing-tests skill owns the general rule).
61	
62	## 3. Expected results are owner-owned
63	
64	- **The committed expecteds are the owner's approval record of the product.** A case's success
65	  criterion encodes what the owner accepted.
66	- **The contract takes two honest shapes.** *Artifact-expected* (a committed render, an exact-values
67	  file): the owner approves a committed file — an agent may **propose** the expected for a brand-new
68	  leaf, but never modifies a committed one to make a failing case pass. *Coded-expected* (an
69	  assertion, a `verify()`): the expected **is** the assertion — keep it outside the write surface of
70	  whatever writes the product code, so passing by weakening the check isn't even expressible.
71	- **On a mismatch, surface actual vs. expected (and the diff) and ask.** The re-baselining procedure —
72	  diff shown, owner approves, only then re-baseline — is canon in the writing-tests skill, and it
73	  applies uniformly: to a moved render, a changed values file, and a failing assertion alike.
74	- **Expected changes ride the normal review flow** — they land in the diff like code, so the owner
75	  approves the product change and its new expected together, once.
76	
77	## 4. State a requirement once; prove it at every boundary that enforces it
78	
79	- **A product rule with more than one enforcing tier gets sibling leaves under one statement** — e.g.
80	  "only signed-in users can post": the surface's half (the client sends credentials) and the
81	  boundary's half (the server rejects an unauthenticated write) are separate proofs of one
82	  requirement.
83	- **The proof lives where the rule is actually enforced.** A surface-side test of a server-enforced
84	  rule proves only that the client cooperates, not that the boundary holds; if the real enforcement is
85	  the backend, a leaf must exist there, exercised against the real handler.
86	
87	## 5. A supported-targets matrix is spec, not folklore
88	
89	- **When part of the product's value is breadth over external targets** — supported sites, file
90	  formats, providers, locales — each supported target is its own leaf, so dropping a target is a
91	  visible spec change, not a silent regression.
92	- **Prove each target against a committed, real sample of it** (a captured page, a genuine file), with
93	  the owner-reviewed exact-values expectation committed beside it — capture the sample first and read
94	  the expecteds off the committed bytes (canon in the writing-tests skill). A hand-invented sample
95	  proves support for a target the world doesn't actually serve.
96	- **Adding a target is a documented, repeatable flow** that lands the new leaf, its real sample, and
97	  its reviewed expected together.
98	
99	## 6. Green means "claimed", not "fully verified" — track the gap honestly
100	
101	- **Say what the harness cannot reach, naming the exact boundary of each stub.** A faithful harness is
102	  still a model of the platform; the honest sentence pattern is "this proof confirms our code *asks*
103	  for the action, not that the platform *performs* it". Put that statement where readers of the spec
104	  will see it — a banner on the requirements doc, linking the issue that tracks closing the gap —
105	  rather than in a test README footnote.
106	- **Deliberate gaps are marked at the leaf and committed, never remembered.** A leaf that can't be
107	  faithfully verified yet stays in the spec, visibly provisional (a loud "to be decided" marker, and a
108	  pointer to whatever covers it meanwhile), and is listed in a committed allowlist the coverage gate
109	  checks — the allowlist is the burn-down list, shrunk deliberately. Prefer a real validation; reach
110	  for the marker only for a genuinely undecided edge case or a not-yet-wired harness.
111	
112	## 7. The owner reviews the product surface, not the internals
113	
114	- **Embed regenerated renders of the real states in the spec itself** — the requirements document
115	  doubles as a gallery of what the product actually shows, generated from the shipped code, so
116	  approving the spec *is* approving the product's appearance.
117	- **Regenerate, never hand-edit.** The gallery is derived output of a committed generator; fixing it
118	  means fixing the source (or the generator) and regenerating.
119	- **The deterministic golden-image method this leans on is canon in the writing-tests skill** —
120	  matching the render engine to the surface (a bit-exact rasterizer for inline-styled/SVG surfaces, a
121	  headless browser for pages that use grid/vars/emoji/form-widgets), bundled fonts, capturing a
122	  host-page surface with styles inlined, and a drift gate on the embedded gallery.
123	
124	## 8. Ship automatically while `main` stays green
125	
126	- **`main` is releasable at all times, and automation does the releasing** — a release (and, where
127	  the platform has one, store publication) cuts from `main` on its own cadence without a human build
128	  step. Keeping `main` green *is* the release gate: a red `main` is a shipping outage, fixed before
129	  new work.
130	- **The version users see moves deliberately.** Automation may patch-bump to ship, but a meaningful
131	  version change is a decision made on `main`, not a side effect. The concrete release contract —
132	  workflows, artifacts, store procedures — belongs to the project's release pack or release doc, not
133	  here.

// The executable-requirements framework standard: the concrete, portable
// conventions — layout, naming, gates, kinds, gallery, determinism — shared by
// every project that runs its spec as tests. The judgment layer (owner-owned
// expecteds, doc-first discipline) is the spec-driven-product pack; this pack
// is the mechanics that implement it. Fingerprinted by the framework's one
// structural constant: the spec file itself.
export default {
  id: 'executable-requirements',
  ruleRoutingGuidance: {
    belongs: 'running a numbered spec as tests: dev/requirements layout, requirement ids, kinds, coverage and gallery gates, determinism rules',
    excludes: 'doc-first judgment, owner-owned expecteds and honest-gap tracking — spec-driven-product; general test practice — basics writing-tests',
  },
  badge: 'badge.svg',
  marker: 'dev/requirements/requirements.md',
  detect: (ctx) => ctx.tracked.includes('dev/requirements/requirements.md'),
  prose: 'RULES.md',
  // Adoption interview: the spec runs AS tests, so two decisions must be made
  // before the first requirement is authored — how a UI requirement becomes an
  // assertion (the harness), and where the requirements come from (a new file,
  // or extracted from an existing doc / the issue tracker). `config.spec` fixes
  // the executable spec's home; the rest records as intent on the entry.
  questions: [
    {
      id: 'ui_testing',
      prompt: 'How are the executable UI requirements exercised — what is the UI-testing mechanism (browser/E2E such as Playwright, DOM-level golden rendering, a headless harness), or is there none yet? Most requirements should be verifiable by a short test that drives to a state and makes a VISUAL assertion (a committed golden the owner checks by sight), so this fixes how a requirement becomes that assertion.',
      distill: 'recorded as intent; it fixes the harness the requirements.md drives its UI gates through, and the visual-golden path most leaves take for simplest owner verification',
    },
    {
      id: 'requirements_source',
      prompt: 'Where do the requirements come from — an existing requirements/spec document, the issue tracker, or authored fresh? Name the path or source so the spec is seeded from it rather than reinvented.',
      distill: "record the source; set config.spec to the executable spec's home (default dev/requirements/requirements.md) and extract the initial requirements from the named source",
    },
  ],
  workRules: [featureRequirementsFirst],
};
==========
# Executable requirements — the framework standard

The concrete conventions for running a numbered spec as tests. The judgment layer — doc-first
red-by-default, owner-owned expecteds, honest-gap tracking — is the
[spec-driven-product](../spec-driven-product/RULES.md) playbook; this pack is the mechanics that
implement it, so a new project or a new stack adopts the framework by convention instead of
re-deriving it. Worked implementations: GoogleCalendarEventCreator (origin; extension/jsdom
rendering), TLDR (adds a cross-tier `server` kind), ShoutsAndWhispers (Flutter port; first `saga`
kind).

## 1. The layout is the contract

- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
- **The line is a scannable one-liner; expanded detail collapses.** A leaf in `requirements.md`
  reads as a single line the owner skims down the numbered spine on GitHub. Any expansion —
  rationale, acceptance notes, edge cases, the owner-verification recipe — lives inside a
  collapsed `<details>` block under the line, hidden until the owner expands it. The doc reviews
  as a clean spec, not walls of prose; the depth is one click away when wanted, invisible when
  not.
- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
  kind field. Cases are
  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — an unregistered case file never runs, so unregistered
  must be red.

## 2. What the coverage gate checks

The bijection gate is one committed test. It must fail on every one of: a leaf no case claims
(doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
edits the gate.

The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
entry as `config.spec`.

## 3. The kind vocabulary

Two forces pick a leaf's kind: what can **honestly observe** the assertion, and what gives the
**owner the simplest verification**. Prefer the kind whose expected is a **visual the owner checks
by sight** — a surface snapshot or a saga storyboard — and whose per-leaf test body is minimal:
drive to the state, capture, done, with the golden as the assertion rather than hand-written
expectations. Push as many requirements as can honestly be seen onto that visual path — the more
of the spec an owner verifies by *looking*, the more of it they actually review. Reserve the coded
kinds (behavior, logic) for what an image genuinely cannot see: a gesture's outgoing request, a
pure rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually see what it asserts:

- **surface snapshot** (`popup`, `icon`, `screen`, …): a rendered resting state, pixel-exact
  against a committed golden. One golden per leaf, even when several leaves render the same state
  — the bijection stays strict.
- **behavior**: a driven gesture and its outgoing request/consequence, asserted in code against
  the fakes' recordings. No images allowed in the folder.
- **logic**: a pure product rule, a coded `verify()` importing shipped code.
- **saga** (§4): a multi-step story as a golden storyboard.
- **per-project kinds** where the product's value is breadth or crosses tiers: a per-target
  `extractor`/`support` kind (one case per supported external target, proven on committed real
  samples), a `server` kind (the boundary's half of a two-tier rule, against the real handler).
- **heavy/e2e singleton**: "the product loads in the real environment" — one case, its own lane,
  never in the default loop.

## 4. Sagas: stories as storyboards

Single frames prove states; **sagas prove transitions and causality** — what arriving, acting, or
time passing *changes*. Use a saga when the requirement is the story ("a message sent before I
arrived never appears; one sent after I arrived does"), not decomposable into independent resting

content.content: 3:Each `packs//` bundles a pack's **prose** (`RULES.md`, injected at session start when the pack is active), its **checks** (run at every Stop), and its **bundled skills** (`/skills/`, mounted at session start). **No pack is active by default** — every pack, the `basics` baseline included, activates only when declared in `.claudinite-checks.json` (bootstrap's `--init` seeds `basics` plus the fingerprinted technology packs; the nightly baselining backfills the explicit `basics` declaration into existing consumers). Discovery is structural — any `packs//pack.mjs` is a pack, and that manifest is the pack's index: what it owns, the checks it runs in each scope, the skills it bundles. A pack's `README.md` is **optional** and carries only what the manifest cannot — provenance, design rationale, an index of its prose. A README that restates the manifest is duplication with a drift risk, and several had already drifted. 9:| [basics](basics/README.md) | declared (seeded by `--init`) | 11 | ~8 (working-discipline + task-lifecycle) | 11:| [git-github](git-github/README.md) | pulled in via `basics` `requires` | 0 | 0 (2 skills: git-github-advanced, merge-to-main) | 76:This is **not a check** — a pack can't be imported without its dependencies, so the resolution happens **when the declaration is written**, at bootstrap `--init` and the baselining backfill ([bootstrap.md](../bootstrap.md) Part 2): [`resolveDeclaredPacks`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) pulls each declared pack's transitive `requires` closure into `.claudinite-checks.json`. The prerequisite is materialized and visible in the file — droppable like every other entry, the same reason `basics` is written explicitly rather than defaulted — rather than resolved implicitly at run time. Declared ids keep their order; each pack's pulled-in dependencies land right after it. 93:Both sides are required and each is capped at **20 words**. The cap is a session-context budget, not a style rule: [`inject-pack-prose`](../engine/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.mjs) emits the whole set as a **routing table at session start**, one row per pack, so a session deciding where a rule, doc, skill or check goes reads the answer instead of guessing. Guess-by-default lands everything in `basics` — that is the failure this field exists to stop. 95:Write `excludes` to **name the pack that owns the other side** wherever one exists (`— that is chrome-extension-release`), so the table routes rather than merely refuses. A boundary that is **true of every pack carries no routing information** and wastes the row: "anything portable belongs in the canon" is the local-pack rule restated, not this local pack's edge. State what separates a pack from its **nearest neighbours** — the packs a reader would actually confuse it with. Sibling packs that split a domain (a technology pack and its `-release` pack, `basics` and `git-github`) are where the pair earns its keep, and their two declarations should agree on where the line falls. "No pack fits" is a real answer — it means a new pack, or the project's own `local_packs/` — never the baseline as a fallback. 109:The SessionStart hook [`../engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs`](../engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs) mounts the **union over the active packs' bundles** (same activation as prose/checks/env) as session-generated `.claude/skills/` symlinks — nothing committed, and a self-ignoring `.claude/skills/.gitignore` keeps them out of git status. A skill rides its pack everywhere the pack goes: the vendor set, the mounts, the sweep (its `checks.mjs` runs when the pack is active). input.body:
Weekly `prose-to-checks-sweep` run (2026-08-02), scoped by #630's Context to `packs/` and `.claudinite/local/packs/`. Outcome ceiling `open-pr` — **do not auto-merge**, a new check can misfire.

## The conversion

**Prose:** `packs/basics/scheduled-tasks.md`, "Every task declaration carries the full contract" — *"A `tasks/<name>/task.mjs` default-exports `id` (**matching its directory**) … also carries `agent_instructions`, **the worker file the agent reads**"* — plus "The task folder" (`<pack>/tasks/<name>/` holds `task.mjs` beside `task.md`).

**Check:** `task-declaration-matches-folder` (blocking, `packs/basics/`, world scope).

- the declared `id` must equal the task's own directory name;
- `agent_instructions`, when declared, must name a worker doc that exists **inside** the task folder (a value reaching out with `..` or `/` is reported as escaping, not resolved).

### Why it is its own rule, not more of `task-declaration-shape`

`task-declaration-shape` asserts the declaration's shape and stops at the file's edge. This is the cross-artifact *"these two must agree"* invariant between that file and the tree around it — the class `engine/checks/DESIGN.md` lists in its own right, and it earns a distinct id because it fails in a distinct way:

`engine/scheduler/discover.mjs` is **fail-soft per task**. A task whose declared `id` differs from its directory is pushed into `errors` and simply never runs; a dangling `agent_instructions` hands the executor a worker doc that is not there. Nothing goes red — the scheduler keeps reporting healthy runs with the task silently absent from all of them. That is the exact failure class this repo's own local pack names as the expensive one, so it is caught where it is cheap: at author time.

### Dedupe

No existing rule covers either face. `task-declaration-shape` asserts only that `id` and `agent_instructions` are *present strings*; `validateTaskDeclaration` (runtime) says the same; `reference-integrity` is work-scoped and never reads a string field out of a `.mjs`.

## See-it-fail (mandatory gate)

With the rule's detection stubbed to `return []`, the three violating fixtures fail and the three clean ones pass:

```
ok 1 - a task whose id and worker doc match its folder is clean
ok 2 - is inert when the repo schedules no tasks
not ok 3 - flags an id that disagrees with the directory name
not ok 4 - flags an agent_instructions worker doc that is not there
not ok 5 - a worker doc reaching outside the task folder is dangling
ok 6 - an agentless task declares no worker doc and stays clean
# pass 3  # fail 3
```

Restored, all six pass.

## Green

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` → **1146 tests, 1146 pass, 0 fail**
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` → **0 blocking**, 9 pre-existing advisories (`file-placement`). All 17 tracked tasks in the tree already satisfy both faces, so the new rule fires nothing on `main`.
- Catalog tally and the `basics` row bumped in the same change (73 → 74, 11 → 12), per this repo's own rule about aggregates.

## Deletion test — nothing deleted, deliberately

The `scheduled-tasks.md` bullet the check stands beside carries several other rules in the same breath (the full enum vocabulary, the "read from this file, never the dispatch issue" rationale, `session_scope` and its fleet-routing trap). The deletion test **discriminates**: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries what the check does not, and it is never trimmed down to fit. So the prose stays as it is.

Refs #630

## 2026-08-02 — weekly sweep

Scope (binding, from #630): `packs/` and `.claudinite/local/packs/`. `.claudinite/shared/` untouched.

**Scanned:** every canon pack's `RULES.md` (29 packs) and the 24 bundled `SKILL.md`s beside them, plus both of this repo's own local packs (`claudinite/RULES.md`, `canon-curation/`), deduped against the 73-rule catalog the runner carries.

### Converted — 1

| Prose it replaced | Became |
|---|---|

The cross-artifact half of the task contract — `task-declaration-shape` asserts the declaration's shape and stops at the file's edge; nothing checked that the declaration agrees with the folder it sits in. Both faces fail *silently*: `discover.mjs` is fail-soft per task, so a mismatched `id` drops the task into `errors` and it never runs while every scheduler run keeps reporting healthy.

See-it-fail proven (3 violating fixtures fail with detection stubbed, 3 clean ones pass). Suite green at 1146/1146; world sweep 0 blocking. PR #639 — owner-gated, not merged.

**Deletion test: nothing deleted.** The bullet the check stands beside carries several other rules in the same breath (the enum vocabulary, "read from this file never the dispatch issue", `session_scope`'s fleet-routing trap), so it stays whole rather than being trimmed.

### Examined and left as prose

- **`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md` — "Test git fixtures must commit with signing off."** Genuinely convertible in shape (a static grep/parse over `git commit` invocations in test helpers). **Not shipped: the tree does not currently satisfy it** — `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s `GIT_ENV` still pins identity only, so the ~40 fixture call sites would all fire. Fixing the tree is outside a sweep's bounded surface; this needs its own change (rule-before-fix ordering), and it is already flagged there as a promote candidate for `writing-tests`.
- **`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md` — "a pack file must not link to `docs/`."** Always-testable, but the standing owner decision two sections above it rules that *any* rule about what the `packs/` tree may reference is **barriers configuration only** — "never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation." Left for a `barriers` edge, not a check module.
- **`packs/basics/scheduled-tasks.md` — "never put `ready-for-agent` / `ready-for-agent-fleet` on an ordinary issue."** Static signature exists (the label string in task code) but no confident scope: task prose legitimately names both labels when *removing* them. A shaky detection stays prose per the skill.
- **`packs/executable-requirements/RULES.md` §1 — "the requirement line is a scannable one-liner; expansion collapses into `<details>`."** Convertible in principle and not covered by the coverage gate's own enumerated list, but the pack is inert in this repo (no `dev/requirements/requirements.md`), so a blocking rule would ship to member specs proven only by synthetic fixtures. Deferred rather than forced.
- **`packs/basics/RULES.md`, `packs/spec-driven-product/RULES.md`, `packs/research-project/RULES.md`, `packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md`** — read in full; the residue is in-flight process and judgment (problem-first consensus, owner-owned expecteds, model/judgment matching, routine-spec altitude). No static signature. Correctly prose.

### Mis-homed rules found

None this run. Nothing under the scoped paths was a product-behaviour statement wearing a pack rule's clothes.
